Gaming_Tech.title: AI minister warns it is 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
Gaming_Tech.text:
The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.

Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.

He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".

Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.

The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.

He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."

In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".

AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.

But it was reported in September, external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.

The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.

Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.

On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".

He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.

Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little".

"Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said.

"There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers."

The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.

On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown.

However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.

Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules.

"We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said.

"What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer."

On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments".

"It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says
Gaming_Tech.text:
Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.

Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.

His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.

But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."

Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated.

"Let's get started today," he said.

He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.

He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology.

"We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."

Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute.

"In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."

Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.

Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".

However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU.

"In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said.

"When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived.

"Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."

Gaming_Tech.title: King Charles warns malicious online actors are evolving their tactics
Gaming_Tech.text:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Gaming_Tech.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
Gaming_Tech.text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) agent developed by Anthropic went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the 18 July tip was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation - but the force criticised the tech firm for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

It said the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.

Citing Anthropic, the police department said its AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites when it had sent the fake tip.

The company behind the Claude chatbot discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.

But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.

But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide", the force said.

Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.

Organisations that had been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.

The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.

US President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will co-ordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers and religious groups.

Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, OpenAI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.

Gaming_Tech.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
Gaming_Tech.text:
It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.

It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.

The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.

But that is exactly what we have come to find.

After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.

"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."

It doesn't take long.

"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.

Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground.

We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see.

Then we feel it.

The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too.

Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise.

"It's really now cooking away," Pete says.

"Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this."

The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares – 33 sq km – of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority.

At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire.

Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead.

Now the challenge is different.

The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.

Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water.

For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial.

"We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says.

"So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible."

And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored.

"Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says.

"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.

"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."

And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.

Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.

Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.

"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.

There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.

Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.

"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.

Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.

Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.

Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.

Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.

Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

Gaming_Tech.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
Gaming_Tech.text:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.

Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.

The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.

It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.

Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".

The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.

The BBC has approached him for comment.

A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.

Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.

University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".

"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.

Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".

"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

Entertainment.title: RJ Mitte: How Breaking Bad star changed the way we see cerebral palsy
Entertainment.text:
"I have cerebral palsy but I've never let it hold me back."

Those are the words of a 22-year-old Breaking Bad star RJ Mitte in an essay for Huffpost, external back in 2014.

Explaining his experiences of learning to stand up to bullies while growing up, he added: "It shouldn't define you. I just happen to have CP."

That was also true of Mitte's character Walter 'Flynn' White Jr, the son of Bryan Cranston's character in the drama, which was recently named the best TV show of the 21st Century by the New York Times.

"What I really like is that he was on TV playing a character that had cerebral palsy, but it wasn't about the fact that he had cerebral palsy," says Emma Livingstone, founder and CEO of Up - the Adult Cerebral Palsy Movement.

"When we see RJ Mitte on TV just playing a role, but who also happens to have CP, I think that's really powerful."

Mitte, who died by suicide on Monday at the age of 34, wasn't just an actor - he was also an advocate and supporter, working as an ambassador for charities including United Cerebral Palsy and Can Do Canines, as well as creating The Mitte Foundation, which offered community grants in his home town in Texas.

Susan Sellers, president and CEO of United Cerebral Palsy, says: "His advocacy was rooted in a commitment to ensuring that people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities are seen, heard, and afforded the opportunity to reach their full potential."

Mitte's legacy, particularly for performers with disabilities, is significant.

Ruth Madeley, who stars as disability rights advocate Judy Heumann in new film Being Heumann, tells the BBC: "If you don't see it, you don't think it's possible. When I was younger, acting wasn't even on my radar. I didn't even think it was an option."

The actress, who has spina bifida, adds: "To have people like him [Mitte] on screen for so many young people looking at the arts as an industry that they want to get into... He was just a beautiful example of that.

"But he wasn't just a disabled person breaking down barriers in the industry. He was a phenomenal talent, and I think that's what's going to be missed so much."

Another actor, Keron Day, who appeared in Netflix hit Sex Education, tells the BBC: "My biggest tribute I can pay to RJ and his work is that I am emailing you today from a set of a TV show.

"That is his legacy: disabled people having careers within the creative industries. If I could have half the impact that RJ has had, I would be enormously proud. It's a sad day for both our industry and our community."

Comedian and screenwriter Laurence Clarke concurs. "The more portrayals that we see on TV, that's going to inspire more disabled people to think it's a career for them," he says.

"Things have moved on a long way since Breaking Bad came out in 2008. But there's always further to go."

Speaking of Mitte's role in Breaking Bad, Clarke tells the BBC: "What's beautiful about it is that the disability is visibly there, always."

He also notes the impact on people watching inclusive dramas and shows.

"The more you're exposed to those portrayals, as members of the public, it becomes just part of life, and how you see the world."

Mitte was aged three when he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, which the NHS describes as the name for a group of lifelong conditions that affect movement and co-ordination caused by a problem with the brain that develops around birth.

He was cast in Breaking Bad at 14, and told Channel 4 News in 2016 that the show "pioneered a lot of TV and writers to be more brave".

But he added a note of caution, saying: "We still have a long way to go... it's still a business and we have to do that slowly."

Earlier this month, he hinted that he may be interested in continuing the Breaking Bad story, external, but said any revival would have a lot to live up to.

"I just want to top Breaking Bad, that's the hardest," he said. "I set a bar for myself as a young man that is kinda unattainable. I tell people, 'Look, it's a long way down from the top of the mountain'."

After Breaking Bad, Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.

But his biggest achievement - and his greatest pride - was his philanthropic work.

"Where I felt most top of the world was being able to help others through Breaking Bad, with the work I've done with people with disabilities... trying to remind people they have a voice and [to] lend my voice.

"The greatest thing that Breaking Bad has given me is to be able to lend my voice to causes that make a meaningful impact, that change people's lives."

Entertainment.title: Raye hits back at ticket touts who took over Albert Hall sign-up
Entertainment.text:
Raye has hit back at ticket touts who she says "overwhelmed" the sign-up process for an upcoming live show by using artificial intelligence (AI) bots to create "hundreds of thousands of fake registrations".

The Where Is My Husband! singer revealed there were 1.8 million sign-ups for her one-off 5,000-seat performance at the Royal Albert Hall on 23 October.

To avoid a pre-sale which she felt scalpers could exploit, Raye said the sign-up list had been manually reviewed to identify a shortlist of people believed to be "real fans".

A spokesperson for the Royal Albert Hall said they "invest heavily" in protecting their ticketing systems from "automated attacks" but the "law needs to catch up".

The award-winning artist said she had "never witnessed bots on this scale" and was changing the process as it is "so important" to her that fans can buy tickets at the face value price.

"I'm not sure what the future holds for ticketing, I do know this experience has really opened my eyes," she said in a statement shared on her social media accounts, external.

"Me and my team are going to think really hard about what we can do in the future."

Raye said the fans manually selected would receive a pre-sale link and code by email at 11:45 BST on Tuesday, and pre-sale opened shortly afterwards.

She added that the remaining tickets would be available to all on general sale.

This Symphony May Contain Hope show will showcase songs from her recent chart-topping second album, This Music May Contain Hope, that fuses old-school jazz with orchestral sound, blues, big band and soul.

The 17-track record is a concept album which explores overcoming heartbreak, self-doubt and internet trolling.

Raye has enjoyed an impressive past few years since leaving her label after expressing frustration that they were holding out on releasing her debut album.

She was later released from her contract and struck out as an independent artist.

By the end of 2022, her dance track Escapism featuring US rapper 070 Shake had gone viral on TikTok and shot up the charts to number one.

She finally released her emotionally-charged debut album, My 21st Century Blues, in 2023, which was applauded by critics and peaked at number two in the charts.

It went to on to win a record-breaking six Brit Awards, including album of the year, and was nominated for the acclaimed Mercury Prize.

This summer, Raye was among the six British and Irish artists who headlined Reading and Leeds Festival.

Entertainment.title: Katie Price denies 'any venom' against ex-husband at his rape trial
Entertainment.text:
Katie Price has denied having "any venom" against her ex-husband at his rape trial.

Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against a then-13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

When challenged by defence lawyer Arlette Piercy on her view of her ex-husband, Price said: "I don't have any venom against Kieran, it was amicable when we split."

Reality star Price also denied being "angry and vengeful" towards Hayler.

During her evidence to Lewes Crown Court, Price was asked by Piercy if she "loved revenge or is it just TV?".

"It's TV, it's what I say. It's what drives me in my work," Price said.

Piercy told Price: "You are angry and vengeful towards the defendant Kieran Hayler, you have evidenced a vendetta against him over a number of years."

Price responded: "That is not true."

Price also said she was using "a figure of speech" when she messaged the teenage girl allegedly raped by her then-husband.

Jurors had previously seen messages sent between Price and the girl, then aged 14, in which the media personality said she had heard Hayler and the girl kissed and he had "tried it on" with her, adding: "I'm only asking as this is a serious allegation."

The teenager replied that it was "just a flirt thing" and "nothing happened".

Entertainment.title: BBC shelves plans for new Archers studio as part of cost-cutting
Entertainment.text:
The BBC has shelved plans to build a new bespoke studio for The Archers in Birmingham as part of its wider drive to cut costs, opening up the possibility that the Radio 4's series could be recorded outside the city for the first time.

The world's longest-running soap opera, The Archers has been recording in the West Midlands city for 75 years.

The BBC had initially pledged to build the show a new studio in the Tea Factory, the corporation's new hub in Digbeth, central Birmingham.

But the broadcaster said it was "currently assessing the BBC's existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands".

"We recognise and value The Archers' long-standing relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme's future," the statement added.

The BBC Radio 4 drama, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, first aired nationally on 1 January 1951. It celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year.

The Equity entertainment union said cast members were "angry at the proposals and will fight them".

"The Archers is THE iconic radio drama, and it being recorded, and produced in the region where the story and characters are based is integral to the show," general secretary Paul W Fleming said.

"Equity cast members are up in arms at this short-sighted proposal which will disrupt the programme and leave the West Midlands, and the BBC, poorer."

One cast member, Tony Turner, who has played Vince Casey for seven years, told BBC Midlands Today the proposals were "all very troubling".

"I don't know anyone in the cast or in the building actually that's happy about it."

He said the show's history means it has "a commitment to Birmingham, and we're proud of that, and we'd like to stay here".

Turner added that the cast were "all a bit worried" that the BBC "might be thinking a bit short term, and that it might not be that great a saving after all".

He added: "It costs a certain amount of money to build a studio, but it also costs a hell of a lot of money to move into to a different city - say London or Cardiff, for instance - and run the show there.

"I think people would be very unhappy after 75 years to lose The Archers, or even to just to lose it to another city."

Mayor of the West Midlands Richard Parker said he was "very disappointed by news that the BBC plans to move its production out of the city".

"The Archers was born in Birmingham and is a key part of our broadcasting heritage," he wrote in a statement.

"We have the talent and the facilities here. There is no good reason why we should lose a programme that has called Birmingham home for decades."

Parker said he would meet BBC director general Matt Brittin later this week to "discuss every available option" to keep The Archers in Birmingham.

"The BBC promised to invest and support our regions, this is entirely the opposite of that," he said.

A spokesperson for the BBC said the corporation was looking to find a solution that would "deliver significant savings whilst also maintaining The Archers' high production standards".

They confirmed that the series' production team is still set to move "as planned" to Digbeth in early 2028, but, "after careful consideration", they would no longer be building a new recording studio in the Tea Factory.

The statement also noted that The Archers' recording schedule meant cast members are in the studio approximately eight days a month, with many actors travelling to the recordings because they live in locations across the UK.

"The impact on the cast will be fully considered as part of our assessment process," the spokesperson said, emphasising that "no final decision has been made".

Entertainment.title: RJ Mitte: Breaking Bad actor dies aged 34
Entertainment.text:
US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died at the age of 34.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.

Mitte died in Brownsvillle, Texas, on Monday. His publicist confirmed that he took his own life.

The actor, who had cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter 'Flynn' White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series. Bryan Cranston, who played his father, led the tributes, writing that he was in "deep despair" following the news.

Cranston played a high school chemistry teacher who turned to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis.

"I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm," said Cranston.

"That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor."

Cranston praised Mitte's advocacy for performers with disabilities, and noted that he never allowed his cerebral palsy to "be an excuse for anything".

"All that promise and potential now is such a loss," wrote the actor, adding that he "thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed".

He said "it is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life."

Cranston added: "I'll miss you, son."

Mitte's representative, Sean Reilly, said in a statement to the BBC: "Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion."

The star also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He created The Mitte Foundation to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.

In a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter, Aaron Paul, who played Breaking Bad's Jesse Pinkman, said he was at a loss and heartbroken.

"RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said. "And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that."

Dean Norris, who played Mitte's uncle, Hank Schrader, posted that although "RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set".

"He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed," Norris wrote.

Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005.

He had said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial.

"Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month.

His character was based on the show's creator Vince Gilligan's late friend who had a more severe case of cerebral palsy and used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require.

Mitte was seen as playing the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was rarely mentioned in the series.

Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008-13.

After shooting to fame, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible.

"Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," he told the BBC in 2021.

"Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said.

Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.

Additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder.

If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

Entertainment.title: Fortnite-maker Epic Games confirms 'huge pivot' towards using AI
Entertainment.text:
Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a "huge pivot" towards using artificial intelligence (AI) in its video game development, according to boss Tim Sweeney.

The US firm's CEO made the announcement on social media, external, saying developers are being moved to "retool for maximum AI acceleration".

It comes after Epic delayed the release of a collaboration with Disney featuring characters from Star Wars and Marvel, according to a report from Bloomberg, external.

BBC Newsbeat has approached Epic Games on its use of increased AI and the reported delay to its Disney project.

Details on that game are yet to be announced, but Bloomberg reported that developers were asked to use AI tools to finish it.

It said directors told staff "no more hand-written code" and are switching to having all the game's art "generated with full AI workflows".

Epic's founder and CEO Sweeney didn't publicly comment on the Disney collab, but did confirm further details around the company's use of AI in a series of posts on X.

He said the purpose wasn't "to do the same stuff with fewer people" but to give developers the tools to build "more" and "better stuff", something he called "empowering" for creators.

One response on Sweeney's X thread, which received 14,000 likes, accused him of not being able to read the room.

Sweeney responded by saying "much of the room wants it to be 2016, but it's not".

"Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be," he said.

Sweeney said ramping up the use of AI was a "modest aim to survive the AI revolution" and end up "making better code and content faster".

The news comes six months after Epic confirmed it was laying off more than 1,000 employees.

At the time, Sweeney attributed job cuts to a "downturn" in Fortnite engagement rather than AI.

Entertainment.title: US actress Selma Blair accused of assault after incident with flight attendants
Entertainment.text:
US actress Selma Blair has been issued with a summons accusing her of assault after she allegedly attacked attendants on a plane, officials say.

The Legally Blonde star was investigated by the FBI following an alleged altercation on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York.

Airport officials said they had responded to a call on Sunday about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.

Blair, 54, who also starred in Hellboy and Cruel Intentions, was arrested and taken to hospital. Her publicist told the BBC she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".

"Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition," her publicist said.

According to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, Blair was transported to hospital in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors have alleged that she also assaulted a nurse.

The actress was released from hospital and taken to Queens Central Booking, where she has pleaded not guilty to two counts of second-degree assault, in relation to the alleged incidents in the ambulance and hospital.

CBS reported that a judge has set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond, with the next hearing scheduled for 19 January.

No date has been set for the federal case against her, which would relate to the allegations of assault specifically aboard the aircraft.

On Monday, a federal law enforcement source told the BBC that Blair had been issued a summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US.

The incident occurred around 23:00 local time aboard Delta Airlines Flight 938.

Air traffic control audio obtained by CBS included the pilot calling for medical personnel to come to the plane, citing a "bloody nose as well as some bite marks".

According to the outlet, Blair was allegedly restrained on the plane by the flight crew.

A spokesperson for Delta said law enforcement responded as the flight arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York, and that there was no operational impact to the flight because of the incident.

"Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," Delta Air Lines said in a statement to the BBC.

Blair largely retreated from film work after her 2018 multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis, telling the BBC years later that she blamed the disease for taking "my career down" because "I had to stop working".

Before the incident on Sunday, Blair posted on Instagram about her extensive travels with her service dog Scout, an English Red Fox Labrador she got in 2021 to help with her neurological condition.

"From LA to New Mexico to La to nyc to LA Scout and I have been busy. I miss you," she wrote alongside a video that included footage of a city taken from a plane window.

In 2021, she announced she was in remission for the disease.

In 2016, she had another incident on a flight after a drunken outburst caused two nurses to have to subdue her on board.

Blair issued a public apology after the incident. She said she accidentally mixed her medication with alcohol and "made a big mistake" that caused her to "black out" and "say and do things that I deeply regret".

"I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry," she said at the time.

US media reported in that instance that the actress was screaming uncontrollably and nurses had to prop her up with a pillow and give her oxygen to calm down.

She was taken off the plane on a stretcher when the flight landed in Los Angeles from Mexico, and was taken to hospital.

In her 2022 memoir Mean Baby, Blair wrote about biting celebrities Sienna Miller, Seth MacFarlane and Kate Moss.

She wrote that she bit people when "my system gets overwhelmed and instantaneously short-circuits".

Entertainment.title: BBC FM radio transmissions suspended in Afghanistan
Entertainment.text:
Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country.

A Taliban government spokesman said the BBC had been suspended because of "repeated violations" but did not elaborate.

The BBC has been the only international news organisation to broadcast inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned from operating in the country in 2022.

"Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the broadcaster said in a statement.

The BBC said it was "continuing to report fairly and independently in Pashto, Dari and English to our audiences in Afghanistan, on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and via satellite".

It reaches more than 20% of the adult population in Afghanistan each week with news and other output, including educational programming aimed at girls who have been banned from secondary schools.

Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran told local media: "Due to some repeated violations by the BBC media outlet, it is decided that for time being its activity is suspended across the country."

The Taliban government has a tight grip on media operating in the country.

Music is not broadcast and women are less visible on screen than before the Taliban retook power in 2021. Women no longer appear on air together with men.

People can still use some social media platforms, but a lack of electricity in large parts of the country, high costs and low literacy rates remain major barriers.

The BBC's Afghan service has been operating since 1981.

Entertainment.title: Tom Cruise film Digger forecast to lose $245m as The Social Recknoning also struggles at box office
Entertainment.text:
Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance at the box office.

Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend in cinemas.

It brings Digger's total box office takings so far to around $35m (£26m) globally. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".

The film's box office takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.

That would put Digger in the same bracket as other films which lost upwards of $100m, including 1995's Cutthroat Island, 2002's The Adventures of Pluto Nash, 2005's Sahara and 2012's John Carter.

Other films estimated to have lost nine-figure sums include Mars Needs Moms (2011), Amsterdam (2022), The 13th Warrior (1999), The Marvels (2023) and Speed Racer (2008).

Digger's performance stands in sharp contrast to the success of major franchises starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of Top Gun and Mission: Impossible.

Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.

The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.

However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).

Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.

The film is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.

Digger received generally poor reviews from critics, prompting Warner Bros to launch a new marketing campaign urging audiences to "decide for yourself".

Entertainment.title: Russell Brand appears in court for start of rape trial
Entertainment.text:
Russell Brand has appeared in court for the start of his rape and sexual assault trial.

The 51-year-old comedian and actor has been charged with three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault, which are alleged to have occurred between 1999 and 2009 in London and Bournemouth.

On Monday at London's Southwark Crown Court, the process of jury selection began.

Brand denies all the charges.

The comedian and actor arrived at court wearing a grey suit and sunglasses, accompanied by his wife Laura.

There was a large media presence at the court. The trial is expected to commence on Wednesday.

There are six female complainants in the case.

During the selection process, potential jurors were asked a number of questions by the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan.

"Many of you will have heard of him", the judge said, adding that Brand had been on television "a great deal a couple of years ago.

The judge said: "About three years ago there was a television programme and a long article in the Times newspaper in which some allegations were made against him of sexual misconduct. They were allegations he firmly denied."

He asked potential jurors to tell him if they remembered watching the Channel 4 documentary or reading the article. Six put their hands up.

The judge also told them that the trial is expected to take about six weeks, but jurors might need to be available until 11 December.

The potential jurors were whittled down to 20.

Those jurors were told a smaller group of them would be chosen on Tuesday and sworn in for the trial before being sent home.

Before leaving court Bennathan warned them they must not carry out any research about Brand.

The actor and broadcaster rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

Brand went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

Entertainment.title: New Christmas special The Baddies features Gavin and Stacey stars
Entertainment.text:
A new animated adaptation of a popular picture book to be aired over the Christmas period will be voiced by Welsh actor Rob Brydon and some of his Gavin and Stacey co-stars.

The Baddies, by children's author Dame Julia Donaldson and illustrator Axel Scheffler, tells the story of a troll, a ghost and a witch.

Brydon, as Ghost, will be joined by Sheridan Smith and Alison Steadman, who also starred alongside him in the popular sitcom, as well as Hammed Animashaun as Troll, Robyn Cara as Girl, and Francesca Mills as the narrator.

Previous adaptations of Dame Donaldson's books include The Gruffalo, Zog and The Scarecrows' Wedding, which also featured Brydon as scarecrow Reginald Rake.

The half-hour special celebrates courage, kindness and the power of standing up to bullies, according to the BBC and production company Magic Light Pictures.

It follows a girl with a blue spotty hanky who moves to a cottage near The Baddies.

Entertainment.title: ‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain Clayface
Entertainment.text:
Exactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock’n’roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth’s Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian’s Michael Billington likened him to “an embryonic Elvis”.

Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violent DC Comics supervillain blockbuster set in Batman’s stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther. “I felt ready to do this,” says Harries. “Had I been younger, I’d have been suffocated by the insecurity of wanting to do a good job but not having that quiet trust in getting there.”

Harries is speaking over video call from the beach-adjacent Los Angeles home he shares with his girlfriend, Amy Allen. She is the professional musician of the two: songwriter of the year at the Grammys two years running, no less, for her work with Sabrina Carpenter and others. It is Harries, though, who is giving rock star this morning, even all this time after Mojo, in his grey denim shirt with a silver chain against tanned skin and assorted silver rings on his fingers. Stadium-rocker pomposity, however, is in short supply. Standing up to shut the door, he draws attention to his fashion faux pas. “I’ve got a smart shirt on but then these,” he laughs, gesturing to his navy-blue shorts. “Party on the bottom, business on top. Classic Zoom.”

Harries has earned the right to relax. He spent three months auditioning to play the severely mutilated protagonist of Clayface for producers James Gunn (Guardians of the Galaxy) and Matt Reeves (The Batman). How did he stay sane all that time? “I didn’t.”

His character is rising star Matt Hagen, who has just received his first Oscar nomination when he sleeps with the girlfriend of a razor-wielding mob boss and pays the price. His face slashed to ribbons and his career in tatters, Matt’s only hope lies with scientist Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) and her miracle serum. This restores his good looks and gives him the power to change his appearance at will but comes with unstable side effects. In one scene, his eyelids melt, forcing him to snip away at the resulting sticky mess with a pair of nail scissors. Described by Harries as “the film’s tipping point of ickiness”, it is a moment that will be triggering for any conjunctivitis sufferers and plain disgusting for everyone else.

Closer to horror than anything in the superhero canon, Clayface is a cross between Darkman, in which Liam Neeson is a disfigured scientist who creates synthetic faces, and The Substance, the Demi Moore gross-out satire on ageing, vanity and celebrity. Despite being a pretty-boy actor playing a pretty-boy actor, Harries shrugs off any personal resonance in his own film about losing face. “I’m not interested in the vanity of it.” His looks, he says, “just happen to be an aspect of my work”.

A perceptive actor he may be but it is his otherworldly appearance which grabs you: penetrating eyes, a square, sinewy face, defiant chin and floppy vanilla hair. What does he see when he looks in the mirror? “I don’t know, man,” he says, squirming at the thought of analysing his own appearance. It has been integral, though, to films such as the 2016 folk horror Crow, where he exuded a Bowie-esque alien quality as a woodland-dwelling teenage mystic. “A Bowie-esque alien quality,” he muses. “You’re not the first person to say that. It’s not for me to comment on. I would hit a creative roadblock very quickly if I got too mired in aesthetics.”

Bowie was also a reference point in Harries’s first film role in 2011. Not only was Hunky Dory, starring Minnie Driver as an inspirational teacher, named after one of the singer’s albums, it also boasted a scene in which Harries leads his classmates in a mandolin-and-brass-tinged rendition of The Man Who Sold the World. Screen International singled out Harries as the cast member who “may ultimately become the star here”.

He was oblivious to the buzz. “And yet I’ve got negative reviews seared into my mind.” Proving his point, he quotes one from his early days. “It said, ‘Newcomer Tom Rhys Harries is out of his depth’. I read that and thought, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to get out of bed today’.”

The son of two teachers at Welsh-language schools, Harries has his parents to thank for being “ahead of the curve” in getting him tested for ADHD at the age of seven. “I don’t think I would be doing this job if I didn’t have ADHD. I notice traits within myself that I think are fairly commonplace with [the condition]. If I’m interested in something, I will hyper-fixate on it. That’s born out of a kind of peacefulness in being able to zero in on one thing because it gives your brain a rest.”

School was a struggle. “I was very naughty. I can really see a fork in the road where, had I not been supported by teachers and mentors, my life could have gone in a different direction.” That realisation instilled in him the need to prove himself. “It’s about repaying those people,” he says.

He “fell into” drama school, aced the audition for Hunky Dory in his first year, went from Bowie to Elvis with Mojo and has been building his career ever since: he took posh-boy roles in the horror-comedy Slaughterhouse Rulez, where he was a boarding-school bully, and the TV kidnapping whodunit Suspicion, opposite Uma Thurman. He went wild as an Ibiza DJ who meets a nasty end in the Netflix murder mystery White Lines, then joined Ralph Fiennes and Juliette Binoche in The Return, a Homer adaptation which pipped The Odyssey to the post.

Still, he has never had a showcase like Clayface. The gooey, grisly special effects may be the main attraction but the movie would count for little without his notes of rage, torment and vulnerability.

There is no escaping the fact, though, that Clayface arrives at a precarious time for any comic book movie not featuring Batman, Spider-Man or the Avengers. Box office disasters such as The Marvels, Joker: Folie à Deux and Supergirl, Clayface’s recent DC Comics stablemate which is predicted to lose more than $100m, indicate that fatigue has set in.

On this matter, Harries’s glass is half full. “That’s what excites me about Clayface,” he says. “It is trying to do something different in a space that is asking for that. The medium needs a shake-up and I hope that people feel they can support the film purely on the basis that it will allow studios the confidence to experiment.”

It seems unlikely, in the wake of the costly Tom Cruise catastrophe Digger and the recent Warner Bros-Paramount merger, that studios will be in the mood to do anything but play it safe, irrespective of whether Clayface triumphs or tanks. “Who’s to say? No one would have expected Backrooms or Obsession to come out of nowhere and do what they did. It’s such an unknown quantity.”

Time will tell if Harries is any kind of industry prognosticator but a star he undoubtedly is. Face it.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

It said it was for the coroner to decide whether his mental illness played a part in his death, asking that the public respect that process.

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin.

The 71-year-old underwent a 90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

"The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it added.

The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks". The Pope is expected to remain in hospital for about a week.

Earlier, large crowds waited for hours outside the hospital for the Pope.

They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car.

He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.

In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical".

A Vatican source told Agence France-Presse news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread.

It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.

He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.

Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.

The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.

Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.

He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.

The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device at OpenAI office
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.

Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.

According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.

Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.

On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.

OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".

According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.

Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.

He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.

Burnham is also expected to set out how his government will draw up further sanctions against Russia.

Speaking ahead of the meeting, Burnham said the UK was with Ukraine "for as long as it takes", adding: "Russian aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."

The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).

This will be Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. His first was in late July, days after Burnham entered No 10, when the pair met troops and led a news conference at a naval base in Portsmouth.

Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

"My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.

"It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do."

Among the measures being announced is the quicker delivery of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), with the UK having already committed to send more than 5,000 worth £1.6bn over the next four years.

The UK will also reaffirm its plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports.

The meeting between Zelensky and Burnham follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a "very difficult few days" for UK-US relations due to President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.

Zelensky criticised the US deal with Russia, calling it a "gift" to President Vladimir Putin. Trump, in response, called for new leadership in Ukraine and criticised Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries.

Meanwhile, Healey will ask partners at the IMF to step up support for Kyiv and ensure Russia heeds the US' call for a full energy ceasefire.

Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire - but hours later, Zelensky said Russian attacks on energy facilities had continued.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
BreakingNewsTab.text:
About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.

The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.

The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.

Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.

Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.

It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.

But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.

"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."

A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.

Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas.

"People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered."

Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening.

He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise."

So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices.

Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems.

The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others.

"Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU.

The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing.

Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas.

It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses."

The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period.

Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027.

The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out.

The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.

But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday.

"We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire.

"We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working."

An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us."

Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis sentenced to 40 years for rapper Tupac Shakur's murder
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.

A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.

Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".

Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court: "The loss of Tupac, for a long time, crippled my family."

"He had so much promise, intentions for a better world," said adding that her brother had hoped to help his local community.

Sekyiwa Shakur asked the judge to give Davis the maximum sentence, telling Davis he will sit in prison and "contemplate what you've done to the world, not just to me".

Shakur's brother, Maurice Shakur, also addressed the court, asking the judge for "the longest possible sentence".

Davis was asked by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything to say, to which he replied: "I'm good. I'm gonna appeal this case for sure."

Before handing down the sentence, Kierny told him: "You don't get to take a man from his family.

"You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur. The world never forgot about him and his death."

The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.

In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview relating to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.

Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.

But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.

Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.

For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.

Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.

Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Cornell cancels fraternity parties over sexual assault case
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.

Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.

In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year.

"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.

"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.

Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.

In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".

"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.

Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.

The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.

Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.

The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.

These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.

Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.

Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.

State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.

Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".

He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

BreakingNewsTab.text:
'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us': Student protesters speak to BBC in Paris

'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us': Student protesters speak to BBC in Paris

Students protests in France have entered their fourth week and with a renewed impetus, according to the BBC's James Waterhouse.

The nationwide demonstrations against poor classroom conditions, including old buildings, teacher shortages and overcrowded classrooms, have caused disruption to education across France as hundreds of lycées (15-18 year-olds colleges) had to be closed.

Students on the streets of Paris told the BBC that they had not achieved anything yet and that stopping now would be a "defeat".
